You explain that there's one way that this is going to go, no devotion or zealotry can overcome the truth of the power of your $shipOrFleet - all ends result in $hisOrHer annihilation, and that of $hisOrHer followers, and of the station.

$HeOrShe has a choice, you explain. Call it a Molochian bargain, if it makes them feel better. Either this is a major loss of personnel, materiel, and the station, or it can be a minor loss of certain assets for a scheme $heOrShe doesn't even really believe in.

Is $heOrShe so loyal to Sedge's sect that $heOrShe is willing to die for it - even after it's already falling apart?
"Well," Bornanew says from beside you. "Let it not be said that you did not attempt diplomacy."
He nods, awaiting your next decision.

You explain that you will require comms buffers and datastores pertaining to Sedge's scheme. You will need the datastores of the nanoforge, and must be given access in order to destroy it.

No one need be hurt; it can be done quickly, without bloodshed, and without compromising $hisOrHer leadership status if $heOrShe secretly gives you their primary security codes. Blame it on the injection of a semi-sentient computer virus, a 'daemon' of the sort Molochians conjure in their AI-labs.

"Why should I trust you to keep your word?" $HeOrShe is clearly unhappy with your terms. "You're no servant of Providence following the holy Word passed to us by Ludd. How can there be light in your heart?"
$HeOrShe looks upon you, face now more open than before, as if almost convinced...

"Cease, I beg you." $HeOrShe puts $hisOrHer head in $hisOrHer hands. "I pray this is the correct Path, that you are not the monster you appear."

"I must accept your terms," $heOrShe says, "I shall pray for forgiveness. And may any hellfire of this world or the next fall upon myself first and not those I seek to protect."

"I admit, I have heard word of the one with whom this deal was struck." $HisOrHer brow furrows. "I cannot say I fully understand it, but we are... requested not to harm you, if it is so possible."

The Pather looks up and away for a moment. "This is a strange Path I find myself walking," $heOrShe says, as if to some greater power. "I pray that its truth may be revealed before long..."

"Your lucre..." A troubled look crosses $hisOrHer face, as if $hisOrHer heart isn't in this condemnation.

"You cannot simply buy your path away from perdition. Many a Mammonite has tried before, and they- they are still judged."

$HeOrShe nods, frowning. "Be that as it may, the corrupt seed of heresy lies in your heart. It is no simple matter to remove such a thing. Your path will take you through blood and pain before it can be pure."

"So it is known," $heOrShe says with a sigh. "You... confound me. Your cooperation with a goon of the Knights, a bully and torturer of a false light... I try to see some greater Plan in it, but I cannot."

"Yours is a path of blood, but there are those who say your soul is not lost to Perdition."

$HeOrShe glares at you sullenly.

"I did not say I was amongst them."
"How lost you are, and how far from the light." $HeOrShe shakes $hisOrHer head, "If the rumors are true, then perhaps some part of you hears a whisper of the Word. That can be the only explanation."

You explain that you will require comms buffers and datastores pertaining to Sedge's scheme. You will need the datastores of the nanoforge as well, and must be given access in order to destroy it.

Few need be hurt, if they cooperate; it can be done quickly and without compromising $hisOrHer leadership status if $heOrShe secretly gives you their primary security codes. Blame it on the injection of a semi-sentient computer virus, a 'daemon' of the sort Molochians conjure in their AI-labs.

"Why should I trust you - you, who threaten me so?"

$HeOrShe is clearly unhappy with your terms. "You're a slave of not only Mammon and Moloch, but Wrath itself. Suffering is your daily bread."
$HisOrHer eyes are watering, $hisOrHer hands wringing. Just one more push should convince $himOrHer...

"Cease your threats!" $HeOrShe puts $hisOrHer head in $hisOrHer hands. "You are a monster out of Hell, and surely that is where I shall find myself for making this deal... but this has gone on long enough. I must protect my people."

"I must accept your terms," $heOrShe says, defeated. "I pray this is the Path."

"Your brutality will only prove how far you are from the Word! Our... our deaths will be as martyrs."

You feel as though $hisOrHer heart isn't quite in it, somehow.

"You persist with that, with that lie," $heOrShe examines you uncertainly.

"Of course, they do say he was shot in the back by a spacer. Maybe the low cunning of your kind makes you capable of such cold-blooded murder."

The Pather frowns. "An obvious boast, typical of a Molochian." $HeOrShe makes a show of looking at you through the comms, "You couldn't have taken Sedge. He was a greater warrior than you or I, by far."

"They do say he was shot in the back by a spacer. The low cunning of you people does suggest your capacity for cold-blooded murder."
"It is true," $heOrShe says ruefully. "Your name is a curse upon the sector. A harbinger of suffering."

"So it is you," $heOrShe says, brow furrowed. "I had thought... surely not... why, pray, would Providence set such evil upon my Path?" 

If anything, $heOrShe looks sad rather than defiant.

And despite your fearsome reputation, you'll let them in on a little secret: it's cheaper, you explain, to accomplish your mission parameters without a fight. Thus the credits you gain, that Mammonite lucre, is ever greater than before.

"I knew it," $heOrShe smirks righteously. "It's always credits in the end with your kind, isn't it."
Cowed by your promises of mercy, the Pather leader provides you with security codes and your ops team mounts what appears to be a lightning-raid which catches the defenders completely by surprise.

Cowed by your promises of mercy - and, perhaps, your credits - the Pather leader provides you with security codes and your ops team mounts what appears to be a lightning-raid which catches the defenders completely by surprise.
Cowed by your brutal posturing, the Pather leader provides you with security codes and your ops team mounts what appears to be a lightning-raid which catches the defenders completely by surprise.

It appears to be "Moloch's own luck," as one captured Pather describes it in the aftermath.

Your teams seize comms buffers, datastores, and a demolitions squad reduces the nanoforge to only so much glowing rubble, spilling jets of atmo and feed-gases into space which occasionally ignite in floral bursts amidst the debris.

The primary defenses are destroyed, the command and control section holed and venting fiery atmo. The superstructure's own spin is pulling the station apart like slow butchery.

You destroyed the nanoforge, but did not secure the evidence Bornanew needed to find the mole in the Cathedral of Holy Exodus on Tartessus.

"It is the best that could be done," Bornanew says, eyes downcast. His notebook is closed, before him. "I must submit myself to the Excubitor Orbis for judgment. On Hesperus."

You convene your officers, and Bornanew, to evaluate the situation.

Pather resistance is expected to be fierce; the core of their militants have a zealous faith, little fear of death, and are often experienced fighters. However they eschew top of the line technology and combat enhancement, whether cybernetic or biochemical.

Bornanew clears his throat and speaks. "Certain classes of combat drugs are accepted among Luddic Path militants. They favor, ah, 'natural' sources." He takes in the confused looks. "Plants," he adds.

Capturing high-value datastores before they're wiped creates exceptional difficulties. The assault must be lightning-quick, and disabling rather than destructive as much as possible.

Pather resistance is expected to be fierce; the core of their militants have a zealous faith, little fear of death, and are often experienced fighters. However they eschew top of the line technology and combat enhancement, whether cybernetic or biochemical.

Capturing high-value datastores before they're wiped creates exceptional difficulties. The assault must be lightning-quick, and disabling rather than destructive so much as possible.

You watch from the command center as marine squads launch the opening salvo from seemingly innocuous cargo containers. Powered armor units burst forth like locusts; combat techs inject malware into the station network, demolitions breach emergency blast doors, and assault teams cut a swath to key targets.

Nodes on the adaptive objective graph, woven through the station tactical display, are achieved one after another. Points blink from blood-red to amber or green, depending on found conditions. Indeed, some comms relays and data clusters auto-destruct upon unauthorized access, but others quietly fail, allowing techs to seize the contents.

The last red-indicated volume is the industrial section housing what is indeed the station's nanoforge; the Pathers had regrouped for a last stand. And so it is.

They were caught off-guard. Despite the large numbers of armed zealots of the Path, your strike teams concentrated force where their defenses, fighting to the death, could not hold.

Teams return to waiting evac drones and shuttles, trailed by tethered spoils: memory blocks torn from their cradles, a few bagged prisoners.

A blue-white flash illuminates the returning victors. Behind them, the industrial section spins itself apart, structural plates shattered into glowing shards, struts tortuously bent, and that atmo which hasn't burned off in a glowing plume forms a rapidly expanding, dissipating cloud, illuminated from within by dying light.

The prize, turned over to your Tech officer's analysis team by a crew of sweating salvors, is a largely uncorrupted backup archive. Standard Domain tech, it hardly looks like the Pathers even knew it was quietly doing its job behind a thin access panel.

The technicians descend upon it with a suite of interfacers, passing every scrap of data to the analysts working in an isolated computing environment to reconstruct the system, starting with comms buffers and metadata.

A cloud of icons, sigils, words forms. Names, front companies, ships, codewords, and references to theological agitprop. Bornanew follows closely, his hands not nearly as deft with the interface as your dedicated techs.

You can see in his body language the exact moment that he finds something he recognizes.

"Keepfaith," Bornanew says. Fumbling with his datapad, the shared workspace highlights all references to that string of letters, then focuses, arranging comms logs and metadata into blocks, compressing everything else down into unobtrusive corners.

He leans back, his eyes darting around some internal catalogue. His paper notebook appears in his hands and he flips to a page as if to check something.
